beats.text: You mention running shoes to a friend over dinner. You never search for them. And the next morning, your Instagram is full of running shoe ads.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: It feels like proof. Your phone heard you.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: Millions of people believe this. Some put tape over their microphones. Some say a product name out loud, just to see if the ads follow.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: So let's decode it properly: the scientists who tested it, the marketing company that bragged about doing it, the times devices really did record people, and how ads seem to read your mind without hearing a single word.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: But first, let's run the famous home experiment. Our host Max is going to try it.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: Max doesn't own a cat. So for one week, he says "cat food" near his phone. At breakfast. On the bus. Very loudly, in the office lift.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: Day one, nothing. Day two, nothing. Day four, there it is: a cat food ad. Max gasps. Case closed?
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: Not quite. Max saw about a thousand other ads that week and doesn't remember a single one. And on day three, he searched "why does my cat food test not work". Oops.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

els.label: MAX SEARCHED
els.big: "why does my cat food test not work"

beats.text: That's the problem with testing it yourself. You count the hits and forget the misses. So let's look at people who tested it properly.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: In twenty eighteen, researchers at Northeastern University in Boston set out to catch phones in the act.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: They used automated software to run more than seventeen thousand popular Android apps, including Facebook's own apps, and they captured every piece of data those apps sent out.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: They were looking for audio leaving the phone. They found none. Not one app secretly switched on the microphone and sent recordings.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: The researchers were careful to say this doesn't prove it never happens. But it was one of the biggest tests of its kind, and it came up empty.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: And they did find something creepy. Some apps were quietly recording the screen and sending videos of what users were doing to other companies.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: One food delivery app, GoPuff, was sending screen recordings to an analytics firm without telling users. It stopped after the researchers got in touch. No microphone needed.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

els.text: stopped after researchers got in touch

beats.text: Facebook has also said, on the record, since twenty sixteen, that it does not use your phone's microphone to choose your ads.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

els.text: "Facebook does not use your phone's microphone to inform ads"

beats.text: Then, in twenty twenty-four, a leak seemed to prove the opposite.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: The news site 404 Media published a sales pitch deck from Cox Media Group, a big American marketing company. It advertised something called "Active Listening".
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

els.text: Cox Media Group pitch deck: "Active Listening"

beats.text: The deck claimed it could use voice data from smart devices to find people who were talking about products, and then target those people with ads.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: Google removed the company from its advertising partner program. Amazon said it had nothing to do with it.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: But a sales deck is not evidence. Nobody has shown that this product worked as advertised, or that it ever ran at any real scale.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

els.text: never shown to work at real scale

beats.text: And here's a strange twist: phones have listened to ads before. Just not to you.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: Around twenty fifteen, a company called SilverPush made code for apps that listened for secret sounds hidden inside TV ads. Whistles too high for humans to hear, but not too high for a phone.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: If your phone heard the whistle, the app knew you had just watched that ad.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: In twenty sixteen, the US Federal Trade Commission sent warning letters to twelve app developers whose apps contained that code, because users were never told.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

els.text: Warning letters to 12 app developers using SilverPush code

beats.text: So the technology to listen is real. What scientists haven't found is phones quietly recording your conversations to sell you shoes.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: There is one place where devices really did record people, though. Voice assistants.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: Your phone listens for one thing only: a wake word, like "Hey Siri" or "Hey Google". A tiny part of the phone checks for it, right on the device.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: But sometimes it mishears. Someone says "seriously" and Siri thinks you called her. It wakes up and records a private conversation by mistake.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: And once the wake word is heard, your request goes to the company's servers to be understood. That's the moment a recording can be stored.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

els.text: where a recording can be stored

beats.text: In twenty twenty-five, Apple agreed to pay ninety-five million dollars to settle a US lawsuit over accidental Siri recordings. Google later agreed to pay sixty-eight million dollars over the same problem with Google Assistant. Neither company admitted wrongdoing.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: Smart speakers have their own stories. In twenty nineteen, Bloomberg reported that thousands of Amazon workers and contractors were listening to Alexa clips to improve it, some reviewing up to a thousand clips a shift.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

els.text: Thousands of Amazon staff listen to Alexa clips

beats.text: And in twenty twenty-three, Amazon paid twenty-five million dollars to settle US charges that it kept children's Alexa voice recordings for years, even after parents asked for them to be deleted. Amazon denied breaking the law.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

els.text: kept kids' recordings after delete requests

beats.text: So the risk is real. But those were accidents, and data kept too long. Not an ad machine listening to your dinner.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: So why don't experts believe your phone is recording everything you say?
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: Let's do some quick maths. Even compressed, voice audio uses roughly sixteen kilobits every second. Over one day, that's about one hundred and seventy megabytes, from every phone, every day.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: Your data pack would notice. Your battery would notice. And security researchers who watch app traffic for a living would definitely notice.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: Phones also warn you now. On an iPhone, an orange dot appears when an app is using the microphone. On Android, a green dot appears, and you can tap it to see which app it is.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

els.text: Android: green dot → tap to see app

beats.text: And it would be a bad deal for advertisers anyway. They already know far more about you than one sentence at dinner could ever tell them.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: So how did the running shoe ad find you? Usually through one of four routes.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: Route one: the people around you. Your friend looked up those shoes after dinner, on the same Wi-Fi. Facebook says it can estimate your location from your internet connection, even with location services off. So ad systems can guess who you spend time with.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: Route two: the trail you leave. Many websites carry a tiny piece of code called the Meta Pixel. When you visit a page, it can report that visit back to Meta, even if you never click anything, and even if you don't have an account.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

els.text: …even if you don't have an account

beats.text: Shops can also upload customer email addresses and phone numbers, and Meta matches them to profiles. That's how a store you bought from once keeps finding you.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: Route three: data brokers and your location. Some apps sell where you go. If your phone visits a gym three times a week, you look like someone who might buy running shoes.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: Route four: your own brain. You see hundreds of ads every day and forget almost all of them. The one that matches a conversation is the one you remember. Psychologists call it the frequency illusion. Just ask Max and his imaginary cat.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: And there's a bonus trick advertisers love: lookalikes. If people who bought running shoes look a lot like you, same age, same city, same apps, you get the ad too. They don't need to know you. They just need to know people like you.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

els.text: same age · same city · same apps

beats.text: Put together, the system doesn't need to hear you. It predicts what you're about to want, sometimes before you even say it.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

els.text: it predicts what you want next

beats.text: Quick game. Real or fake? I say a phone myth, you decide.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: Myth one: airplane mode stops all tracking. Fake. Many apps simply save what you did and send it the moment you reconnect.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

els.text: apps send it when you reconnect

beats.text: Myth two: incognito mode hides you from websites. Fake. It only stops your own phone from saving your history. Websites, and your network, can still see you.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

els.text: only your own history is not saved

beats.text: Myth three: your phone is always listening for one thing. Real. The wake word. That's why turning it off is one of the simplest privacy wins.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

els.text: the wake word · turn it off = easy win

beats.text: Myth four: a sticker on your camera also blocks the microphone. Fake. They're separate parts. The sticker does nothing for the mic.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: What about India? Our data protection law, the DPDP Act, finally has its rules in place since November twenty twenty-five.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

els.text: DPDP Act rules in place since November 2025

beats.text: They roll out in phases until twenty twenty-seven. Companies will have to tell you clearly what data they collect and why, and let you withdraw your consent easily.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: Until then, here is what you can do today, in about five minutes.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: One. Check which apps can use your microphone. On iPhone, go to Settings, Privacy and Security, Microphone. On Android, open the Privacy dashboard. Switch off anything that doesn't need it.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: Does your torch app need your microphone? Does your calculator? No. Switch them off.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: Two. Watch for the dot. If the orange or green dot appears when you're not on a call or recording, find out which app is using it.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

els.text: not on a call? find the app

beats.text: Three. Limit ad tracking. On iPhone, choose "Ask App Not to Track". On Android, delete your advertising ID in Settings.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: Four. On Facebook and Instagram, open your activity off Meta technologies, and disconnect the websites that report on you.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: Five. If voice assistants worry you, turn off the wake word, and review or delete your saved voice recordings.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: So, is your phone secretly listening to you? Almost certainly not, at least not for ads.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: The uncomfortable truth is that it doesn't need to. Your searches, your location and the people around you already tell the story.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: And Max? He's buying cat food anyway. The ads won.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

beats.text: Tell me in the comments: what's the creepiest ad you've ever seen?
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace

els.label: YOUR COMMENT
els.big: The creepiest ad I ever saw…

beats.text: And subscribe to TechDecoded with Max for more tech, decoded.
beats.dir: clear, engaging explainer tone, natural pace
